extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, critics, and readers interested in principles of architectural design and ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive aesthetic and practical guidance for designing and evaluating architecture—focusing on proportion, ornament, workmanship, and the memorial/durable character of buildings. Uses examples (St. Mark's, Bayeux, Rouen, Ferrara, etc.) to illustrate principles such as variation, hand-work, finish, and the civic duty to build to last.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportioning of shafts and arches
rubrics_metrics.description: The height of the lower shafts, upper shafts, and wall being severally expressed by a, b, and c then a:c :: c:b (a being the highest); the diameter of shaft b is generally to the diameter of shaft a as height b is to height a, or something less, allowing for the large plinth which diminishes the apparent height of the upper shaft; in the extreme arches a single under shaft bears two upper, proportioned so that the diameter of each upper = 2/3 of lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed proportional relationships should govern vertical composition so that the lower story attains three terms of proportion and the upper adds a third term in pinnacles; proportions may be subtle and varied across the facade (example: St. Mark's). Measuring exact dimensions may be complex, but the intended harmonic relationships between heights and diameters are essential to visual harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical and lateral division to secure overall form
rubrics_metrics.description: Facade composed of upper and lower series of arches with ranges of shafts creating five vertical divisions (two tiers of shafts and the arched wall they bear below; one tier and arch above), and lateral divisions that diminish in alternation to secure a pyramidal whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should manage both vertical tiers and lateral sequence of arches (e.g., seven lower arches diminishing in order a, c, b, d) so that while parts ascend or descend proportionally, the whole retains a pyramidal or unified form. Avoid mechanical mirroring; aim for musical interplay of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective symmetry achieved by deliberate variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in apparent symmetry (e.g., northern b and c wider than southern b and c; southern d wider than northern d) are not blunders but deliberate methods to achieve effective symmetry by nuanced differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects may intentionally avoid exact replication between corresponding members to create life and subtlety; differences should feel like natural growth rather than careless error (examples: St. Mark's, Bayeux, Abbeville). Do not mistake deliberate asymmetry for incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design by feeling rather than slavish rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: The Byzantine workmen built altogether from feeling, not by enumerated principles; it was because they built from feeling that there is marvellous life, changefulness, and subtlety in their arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize aesthetic judgement and an intuitive sense of harmony over rigid adherence to measurement protocols. Feeling-based decisions can produce organic vitality; yet they require cultivated taste and understanding of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courageous departures and meaningful ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Daring variation of pretended symmetry and departures from common habits (e.g., ugly beehive in place of a principal niche, or extraordinary sculptural placement in St. Maclou) can be justified when they serve a peculiar meaning or dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconventional elements may be employed where they add expressive meaning or bind composition into one mass. Such licences require courage and intention; they may be 'ugly' by some standards but can contribute vitality when thoughtfully used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality of Assimilation (readiness to adopt diverse motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty which turns to its purposes all material that is submitted to it—adopting ideas and resemblances from any sources whatsoever (example: Ferrara columns inspired by an awning rack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects should be open to humble or unexpected sources for ornament and form; humility in borrowing and boldness in departing from established types can produce harmonious, lively work. Imitation of merely mechanical forms is not exemplary—assimilation should transform source motifs into living architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-work versus machine-work: value of the living hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-work may always be known from machine-work; so long as men work as men, putting their heart into what they do, there will be handling 'above all price'—pauses, varied chisel strikes, and localized care that set off parts of a composition. Machine or lifeless work shows a cold, equal trouble everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer craftsmanship that reveals human feeling: deliberate unevenness, pauses, and expressive touches. Beware uniform, cold, 'polished' finishes that equalize attention across the work (anti-pattern: engine-lathe-level regularity). The difference may be imperceptible to some, but crucial to lovers of architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right finish and high finish defined by intended impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Right finish is simply the full rendering of the intended impression; high finish is the rendering of a well-intended and vivid impression; oftener got by rough than fine handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish should be driven by the expressive aim, not by a fetish for polish. Aim to render the intended emotional or visual effect—sometimes rough, vivid touches achieve this better than smooth, equal polishing. Avoid equating completeness with smooth gloss produced by sandpaper or machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture as painting with the chisel
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture is not the mere cutting of the form of anything in stone; it is the cutting of the effect of it—half the touches are to put power into the form, to create light and shadow rather than literal ridges and hollows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptors should employ chiselling to produce lines of light and spots of darkness, using seemingly rude or angular touches to intensify expression (examples: Mino da Fiesole, statues of St. Lorenzo). Avoid over-literal, photographic carving; prioritize the effect produced at viewing distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompletion used as an expressive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Incompletion itself can be a means of additional expression; touches that are rude and few by a regardful mind differ greatly from careless incompleteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate partial finishing can enhance vitality—use incompletion where it emphasizes the intended impression. Distinguish between thoughtful economizing of finish and mere negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be made with enjoyment and love
rubrics_metrics.description: The right question respecting all ornament: Was it done with enjoyment—was the carver happy while he was about it? If the men who did it hated it, it will be dead and lifeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that ornament design and execution are undertaken by craftsmen who take pleasure in their work. Anti-pattern: details designed with taste but executed by craftsmen who hate the work, producing dead ornament. The emotional state of makers matters to the life of ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject superficial stamped and imitation ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: All the stamped metals, artificial stones, imitation woods and bronzes, and other short, cheap, and easy ways of doing difficult work are new obstacles—they will not extend pride of judgment or enjoyment but make us shallower and colder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prefabricated, stamped, or imitation decorative elements; prioritize authentic materials and handcraft even if more costly. These machine-made shortcuts reduce depth of understanding and weaken architectural life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for geometrical color-mosaic as viable ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Given current powers of sculptural ornament, the only manner of rich ornament open may be geometrical color-mosaic, which much might result from if strenuously taken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sculptural craft is limited, consider geometrical color-mosaic as an alternative to produce rich ornamentation; it can achieve richness without depending on fragile or poorly executed carving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cold uniformity and equalized labour in finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold cutting—the look of equal trouble everywhere—the smooth, diffused tranquillity of heartless pains—is characteristic of machine or lifeless work and is to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek perfectly uniform treatment across all parts; allow contrasts of attention and finish so that some parts are more delighted-in than others. The chill often shows in finished work as a sameness that kills expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as memory: buildings should be memorial/monumental
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture is the centralisation and protectress of sacred influence; we may live without her, but we cannot remember without her. There are two duties: to render the architecture of the day historical, and to preserve that of past ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design buildings (civil and domestic) with the intention that they may serve as records and memorials of a people's life—use stable materials and meaningful decoration so buildings contribute to national memory and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic buildings should be built to last and be monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an evil sign when houses are built to last for one generation only. A good man's house should be a temple; houses should be built to stand as long as human work can be hoped to stand and to record to their children what the builder has been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor durable construction, patient completion, and designs that allow dwellings to act as warm monuments to family life. Avoid ephemeral, cheaply-built tenements that reflect social instability and disregard for home as sacred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right scale: small houses can be most exquisite
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a house must be large in order to be well built is modern; some of the most exquisite buildings are small—many notable Venetian and Italian examples are ground floor plus two stories with few windows yet of great beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate grandeur with size—good design and careful detail can make small houses historically and aesthetically rich. Emphasize proportion, ornament, and thoughtfulness over mere scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow houses to bear inscriptions and be personalized monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank stones should be left in places to be inscribed with a summary of the builder's life and experience, raising habitations into monuments and developing instructiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate means for personal or historical inscription into domestic design so that houses can be memorials. This strengthens familial continuity and civic memory.
